confirmed.statement: Caveat, no code change. The paper describes no randomization procedure and reports no balance test on Table I. Table I puts all eight 18-year-olds in the control group (0 of 58 vs 8 of 55). Under random allocation into groups of 58 and 55, a split this extreme has probability 0.002 (two-sided Fisher exact test, my calculation), although this cell was picked after seeing the table. The baseline AUT check 'to assess whether their creativity levels were comparable' is reported before the sentence on random assignment and does not name the groups it compares. The form notes the AI-experience differences in Table I but not the age split. These points weaken confidence in how assignment was done. They do not contradict the paper's explicit statement of random assignment.

summary: The PDF explicitly supports every part of the assignment, arms, and ai_tool coding: in a between-subjects design, 113 undergraduates were randomly assigned to draw an alien with the Kimi.AI web interface pre-opened in a computer-equipped laboratory (58) or independently without GAI tools (55), and two coders rated the participants' own drawings (PDF pp. 1-4, Sections II.A-II.C, Tables I-II). The caveats leave criterion 1 intact but weaken confidence in how assignment was done: the paper describes no randomization procedure, tested the arms separately, and its Table I puts all eight 18-year-olds in the control group (two-sided Fisher exact p = 0.002, my calculation).
